scenes.text: When the universe was very young, it made matter and antimatter in almost exactly equal amounts.
And when matter meets antimatter, both of them disappear. All that's left is a flash of light.
So by now, the universe should be empty. No stars, no planets, no people. Just a faint glow of light, spreading out forever.
But it isn't empty. Because the two amounts weren't quite equal.
For every billion particles of antimatter, there were about a billion and one particles of matter.
The billions met and destroyed each other. The one in a billion was left over. And everything you have ever seen is made of that leftover.
We even know the ratio. The early universe left behind a faint glow that still fills space. For every proton and neutron, there are more than a billion particles of light.
Why the extra one? Nobody knows yet. Our best theory of particles allows a tiny imbalance, but nowhere near enough.
Physicists are hunting for the rest. One suspect is the neutrino, the particle that passes through almost everything.
But even if they solve that puzzle, that would only tell us why there's matter instead of just light. Not why there's anything at all.
Why is there a universe to make matter in? Why is there something, instead of nothing?
In 1714, the German philosopher Gottfried Leibniz asked exactly that. And he added something that sounds simple, but isn't.
Nothing, he wrote, is simpler and easier than something.
At first glance, nothing seems easier to explain. No rules, no beginning, no cause. With something, all three come up.
So the strange thing isn't that the universe is weird. It's that there's a universe at all.
Physics has several ideas about where the universe came from. But there's a problem with every one of them. They all start with something.
Let's start with the easiest version of nothing. Take a box. Remove everything inside it.
Every atom. Every speck of dust. Every particle of light. Cool it down as far as physics allows.
That's nothing, surely. Empty space.
It isn't. According to quantum physics, empty space is full of fields, and those fields can never be perfectly still.
They keep trembling, even in their lowest possible state. That lowest state is called the vacuum. And the vacuum is busy.
You can even measure it. Put two metal plates in a vacuum, far less than a hair's width apart, and they get pushed towards each other.
Nothing touches them. In the usual picture, the push comes from the vacuum itself. It's called the Casimir effect, after the Dutch physicist who predicted it in 1948.
And that gave some physicists an idea. If empty space is restless, maybe a whole universe could come out of it.
In 1973, the physicist Edward Tryon asked whether the universe might be a fluctuation of the vacuum.
But where would the energy come from?
Maybe it doesn't have to. Matter carries positive energy. Gravity, in a sense, carries negative energy. Add them up, and the total might be exactly zero.
In 2012, the physicist Lawrence Krauss wrote a bestselling book on this idea. Its title was "A Universe from Nothing".
And a philosopher of physics, David Albert, wrote a review that went straight for the title.
Quantum fields, he pointed out, aren't nothing. They're stuff. Stuff that follows laws.
That explains how the house was built. It doesn't explain the bricks.
So take away even more. No vacuum. No fields. No space at all, and not even time.
In 1982, the physicist Alexander Vilenkin described a universe that appears with no space and no time before it.
In his model, a tiny universe appears through a quantum process called tunnelling. Then it starts to expand.
This is one of the closest things physics has come to nothing.
But the laws of physics are still there. They allow the universe to appear. And nobody has explained why those laws exist in the first place.
Each step took something away. None of them got to zero.
Physics describes how one state changes into another. But every explanation needs something to start with.
A state. A rule. Something. True nothing has none of these. And that's where physics reaches its limit.
In 1948, on BBC radio, the philosopher Bertrand Russell debated this with a Jesuit priest, Frederick Copleston.
Copleston started with the things around us. Stars, planets, people. None of them had to exist. Each could have been otherwise.
Philosophers call that contingent. Something that exists, but could have failed to.
And Copleston argued that adding up contingent things doesn't help. The whole universe is contingent too. It can't be the reason for itself.
So, he concluded, something must exist necessarily. Something that could not have failed to exist, and needs no reason beyond itself. For Copleston, that was God.
It's the answer Leibniz gave too. And notice what it does to the question "what explains God?" For Copleston, that question doesn't arise. A necessary being is where the questions stop.
Russell wasn't persuaded. Every person who exists has a mother, he said. That doesn't mean the human race has a mother.
Each thing in the universe may need a cause. That doesn't mean the universe as a whole needs one.
And he doubted that "necessary" could apply to a thing at all. Only statements can be necessary, he said. Not things.
Russell's own view was simpler. The universe, he said, is just there, and that's all.
To Copleston, that was refusing to play. Years later, he wrote that if you won't even sit down at the chessboard, you can't be checkmated.
For Copleston, the chain of reasons ended in God. For Russell, there was no further explanation to give.
And physics doesn't escape this either. If a law explains the universe, what explains the law? Each of these chains ends somewhere. The question is where.
There's another way out, and it turns Leibniz upside down.
In 1996, the philosopher Peter van Inwagen asked how many ways a world could be.
There are endlessly many ways for there to be something. One star, or two, or a billion. Different laws, different everything.
But there's only one way for there to be nothing.
His idea was simple. If every way a world could be were equally likely, the empty one would practically never come up.
Leibniz thought nothing was the simplest state of all. Van Inwagen thought it was far less likely than something.
Not everyone is convinced. Why should every possibility be equally likely, like tickets in a lottery? And endless possibilities don't come with odds attached.
And maybe the question itself is stranger than it looks. Ask what nothing is like, and you're already treating it as a kind of something.
Physics can tell us a lot. One day, perhaps, why there's matter. How a universe might grow from almost nothing.
What it can't tell us is why there's anything for its laws to be about.
And philosophy hasn't settled it either. Every explanation we've heard either starts with something, or stops at something. This is where explaining itself runs out.
At least one small part of that universe can now ask why it exists.
Nothing can't wonder why there's something. Only something can.
So here's a question for you. Is "the universe is just there" an honest answer, or a way of not answering? Let me know in the comments.
